rationale: A wins because it separates real press lanes and marks the weak spots instead of decorating them. A's "$550 per flight: the savings number Going's paid tier rests on" is a narrow money angle a personal-finance editor can interrogate; B's "The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" spins one old-name fact into a soft identity arc. B has usable bones, but it keeps asking verification to rescue claims it already made.
gaps_in_A: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is a reasonable industry instinct, but it is not stated in the update. Keep it only with a real member example or data on fare-expiration urgency.
The paywall angle asks for "the actual size of the Premium/Elite base" but misses Premium/Elite price. A subscription-business reporter will ask whether the upsell math clears the subscription cost.
"If the prevailing push in the space is toward agents that book end-to-end" is correctly caveated, but still cannot be pitched until live competitive coverage proves that premise.
gaps_in_B: "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" and "most AI trip planners start from a user's query" are outside the supplied facts. Verify first; don't make the unsupported comparison the spine of Angle 1.
"The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" is profile mush. The update gives an old name, not a sourced rebrand arc, platform strategy, or product-history story.
"A tech reporter or columnist" is not a clean journalist shape. That is an inbox label, not a beat.

Rejecting "Going's premium members save an average of $550 per flight" as "slop" throws away a viable personal-finance/data angle. The right move is to demand methodology, not bury the only hard dollar figure in the update.
